decisions.mark: describes the external bridge's two-level thread structure: one accept thread that spawns a further thread per connected client
decisions.detail: QUOTE: External MCP accept loop | `src/facade/external_bridge.cpp:796` | Joined in `stop()`; Per-client serve threads | `external_bridge.cpp:945` | Shut down via `shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` and joined in `stop()` | WHY: The answer lists an accept-loop thread and separate per-client serve threads in the external bridge, which gives the two-level structure of an accept thread plus one thread per client. || QUOTE: External MCP accept loop | `src/facade/external_bridge.cpp:796` | Joined in `stop()` ; Per-client serve threads | `external_bridge.cpp:945` | Shut down via `shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` and joined in `stop()` | WHY: The table names an accept-loop thread and separate per-client serve threads in the external bridge, with `stop()` shutting down client sockets and joining, which conveys the two-level structure. || QUOTE: External MCP accept loop | `src/facade/external_bridge.cpp:796` | Joined in `stop()` | Per-client serve threads | `external_bridge.cpp:945` | Shut down via `shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` and joined in `stop()` | WHY: The answer lists an accept-loop thread and separate per-client serve threads in the external bridge, and its stop() description (stops accepting, shuts down client sockets, then joins) covers the two-level structure, though it doesn't say outright that the accept thread spawns the client threads.

decisions.detail: QUOTE: "HealthMonitor queues events under `event_mutex_` and runs the status callback only from `process_events()`, so callers never see a callback on the monitor thread (`health_monitor.cpp:118`)." | WHY: The answer states events are queued under a mutex and the callback runs only from process_events(), not on the monitor thread. || QUOTE: "HealthMonitor queues events under `event_mutex_` and runs the status callback only from `process_events()`, so callers never see a callback on the monitor thread (`health_monitor.cpp:118`)." | WHY: The answer states the monitor queues events under a mutex and the callback runs only from process_events(), not on the monitor thread. It doesn't say outright that process_events() is drained on the caller's thread, but the heading "Callbacks on the engine thread" and "callers never see a callback on the monitor thread" carry that.
